also_in: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland) (1915)
The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)
The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Draw a pail of water
text:
Draw a pail of water,
For my lady's daughter;
My father's a king, and my mother's a queen,
My two little sisters are dressed in green,
Stamping grass and parsley,
Marigold leaves and daisies.
One rush! two rush!
Pray thee, fine lady, come under my bush.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Jack and Jill
text:
Jack and Jill
Went up the hill,
To fetch a pail of water;
Jack fell down
And broke his crown,
And Jill came tumbling after.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Tell Tale Tit
text:
Tell Tale Tit,
Your tongue shall be slit;
And all the dogs in the town
Shall have a little bit.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Goosey, goosey, gander
text:
Goosey, goosey, gander,
Where shall I wander?
Up stairs, down stairs,
And in my lady's chamber:
There I met an old man,
Who would not say his prayers;
Take him by the left leg,
Throw him down the stairs.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Willy boy, Willy boy, where are you going
text:
Willy boy, Willy boy, where are you going?
I will go with you, if I may.
I'm going to the meadow to see them a mowing,
I'm going to help them make the hay.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Bonny lass, pretty lass, wilt thou be mine
text:
Bonny lass, pretty lass, wilt thou be mine?
Thou shall not wash dishes,
Nor yet serve the swine;
Thou shalt sit on a cushion, and sew a fine seam,
And thou shalt eat strawberries, sugar, and cream!
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: A dillar, a dollar
text:
A dillar, a dollar,
A ten o'clock scholar;
What makes you come so soon?
You used to come at ten o'clock,
But now you come at noon!
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)
also_in: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland) (1915)
The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Little Betty Blue
text:
Little Betty Blue,
Lost her holiday shoe.
What will poor Betty do?
Why, give her another,
To match the other,
And then she will walk in two.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Girls and boys come out to play
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Rock-a-bye baby
text:
Rock-a-bye baby,
Thy cradle is green;
Father's a nobleman,
Mother's a queen.
And Betty's a lady,
And wears a gold ring;
And Johnny's a drummer,
And drums for the king.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Little Tom Tucker
text:
Little Tom Tucker,
He sang for his supper.
What did he sing for?
Why, white bread and butter.
How can I cut it without a knife?
How can I marry without a wife?
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Little lad, little lad
text:
Little lad, little lad,
Where wast thou born?
Far off in Lancashire,
Under a thorn;
Where they sup sour milk
From a ram's horn.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Little maid, little maid
text:
Little maid, little maid,
Whither goest thou?
Down in the meadow
To milk my cow.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: My mother, and your mother
text:
My mother, and your mother,
Went over the way;
Said my mother, to your mother,
"It's chop-a-nose day."
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: All around the green gravel
text:
All around the green gravel,
The grass grows so green,
And all the pretty maids are fit to be seen;
Wash them in milk,
Dress them in silk,
And the first to go down shall be married.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: One foot up, the other foot down
text:
One foot up, the other foot down,
That's the way to London town.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Tom, Tom, the piper's son
text:
Tom, Tom, the piper's son,
He learnt to play when he was young,
He with his pipe made such a noise,
That he pleased all the girls and boys.
source: Mother Goose or the Old Nursery Rhymes, ill. Kate Greenaway (Warne)

title: Cock-a-doodle-doo
text:
Cock-a-doodle-doo,
My dame has lost her shoe;
My master's lost his fiddlestick,
And knows not what to do.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: Peter, Peter, pumpkin eater
text:
Peter, Peter, pumpkin eater,
Had a wife and couldn't keep her;
He put her in a pumpkin shell,
And then he kept her very well.

Peter, Peter, pumpkin eater,
Had another, and didn't love her;
Peter learned to read and spell,
And then he loved her very well.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: I like little pussy, her coat is so warm
text:
I like little pussy, her coat is so warm,
And if I don't hurt her she'll do me no harm;
So I'll not pull her tail, nor drive her away,
But pussy and I very gently will play.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)
The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: I'll tell you a story
text:
I'll tell you a story
About Mary Morey,
And now my story's begun.
I'll tell you another
About her brother,
And now my story's done.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Dickery, dickery, dock
text:
Dickery, dickery, dock,
The mouse ran up the clock;
The clock struck one,
The mouse ran down,
Dickery, dickery, dock.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: H, I, J, K, L, M, N, O, P,
text:
Q, R, S, and T, U, V,
W, X, and Y and Z.
Now I've said my A, B, C,
Tell me what you think of me.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: About the bush, Willie, about the bee-hive
text:
About the bush, Willie, about the bee-hive,
About the bush, Willie, I'll meet thee alive.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: There was an old man
text:
There was an old man,
And he had a calf,
And that's half;
He took him out of the stall,
And put him on the wall,
And that's all.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)
The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Bow, wow, wow
text:
Bow, wow, wow!
Whose dog art thou?
Little Tom Tinker's dog,
Bow, wow, wow!
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: There was an old woman lived under the hill
text:
There was an old woman lived under the hill,
And if she's not gone she lives there still.
Baked apples she sold, and cranberry pies,
And she's the old woman that never told lies.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Sing a song of sixpence, a bag full of rye
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: There were two birds sat upon a stone
text:
There were two birds sat upon a stone,
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
One flew away and then there was one,
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
The other flew after and then there was none,
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
So the poor stone was left all alone,
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
One of these little birds back again flew,
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
The other came after and then there were two,
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
Says one to the other: "Pray, how do you do?"
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
"Very well, thank you, and pray how are you?"
Fal de ral-al de ral-laddy.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Bye, Baby bunting
text:
Bye, Baby bunting,
Father's gone a-hunting,
Mother's gone a-milking,
Sister's gone a-silking,
And Brother's gone to buy a skin
To wrap the Baby bunting in.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Pussy cat, pussy cat, where have you been
text:
Pussy cat, pussy cat, where have you been?
I've been to London to see the Queen.
Pussy cat, pussy cat, what did you there?
I frightened a little mouse under the chair.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Pat a cake, pat a cake, Baker's man
text:
Pat a cake, pat a cake, Baker's man;
So I do, master, as fast as I can.
Pat it and prick it and mark it with T,
And then it will serve for Tommy and me.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: There was an old woman tossed in a blanket
text:
There was an old woman tossed in a blanket
Seventeen times as high as the moon;
But where she was going no mortal could tell,
For under her arm she carried a broom.

"Old woman, old woman, old woman," said I,
"Whither, ah whither, ah whither so high?"
To sweep the cobwebs from the sky,
And I'll be with you by and by."
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: Cold and raw the north winds blow
text:
Cold and raw the north winds blow
Bleak in the morning early,
All the hills are covered with snow,
And winter's now come fairly.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: "To bed, to bed," says Sleepy-Head
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Is John Smith within?--Yes, that he is
text:
Is John Smith within?--Yes, that he is.
Can he set a shoe? Ay, marry, two.
Here a nail and there a nail,
Tick--tack--too.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: When I was a little boy I lived by myself
text:
When I was a little boy I lived by myself,
And all the bread and cheese I got I put upon a shelf;
The rats and the mice, they made such a strife,
I was forced to go to London to buy me a wife.
The streets were so broad and the lanes were so narrow,
I was forced to bring my wife home in a wheelbarrow;
The wheelbarrow broke and my wife had a fall,
And down came the wheelbarrow, wife and all.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Little Jack Horner
text:
Little Jack Horner
Sat in a corner
Eating a Christmas pie;
He put in his thumb,
And pulled out a plum,
And said: "Oh, what a good boy am I!"
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: Miss Jane had a bag and a mouse was in it
text:
Miss Jane had a bag and a mouse was in it;
She opened the bag, he was out in a minute.
The cat saw him jump and run under the table,
And the dog said: "Catch him, Puss, soon as you're able."
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Goosey, goosey, gander, where dost thou wander
text:
Goosey, goosey, gander, where dost thou wander?
Upstairs and downstairs and in my lady's chamber;
There I met an old man that wouldn't say his prayers,
I took him by his hind legs and threw him downstairs.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: See saw, Margery Daw
text:
See saw, Margery Daw,
Jacky shall have a new master:
Jacky must have but a penny a day
Because he can work no faster.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: The lion and the unicorn
text:
The lion and the unicorn
Were fighting for the crown.
The lion beat the unicorn
All about the town.
Some gave them white bread,
And some gave them brown;
Some gave them plum-cake,
And sent them out of town.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Bonny lass, pretty lass
text:
Bonny lass, pretty lass,
Wilt thou be mine?
Thou shalt not wash dishes
Nor yet serve the swine.
Thou shalt sit on a cushion
And sew a fine seam,
And thou shalt eat strawberries,
Sugar and cream.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: Handy-spandy, Jacky dandy
text:
Handy-spandy, Jacky dandy,
Loves plum cake and sugar candy.
He bought some at a grocer's shop,
And pleased away went hop, hop, hop.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: Ding--dong--bell, the cat's in the well
text:
Ding--dong--bell, the cat's in the well.
Who put her in? Little Johnny Green.
Who pulled her out? Great Johnny Stout.
What a naughty boy was that
To drown poor pussy cat
Who never did him any harm,
And killed the mice in his father's barn.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: This pig went to market
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: There were two blackbirds sitting on a hill
text:
There were two blackbirds sitting on a hill,
One named Jack and the other named Jill.
Fly away, Jack! Fly away, Jill!
Come again, Jack! Come again, Jill!
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: Pease-porridge hot
text:
Pease-porridge hot,
Pease-porridge cold.
Pease-porridge in the pot
Nine days old.
Spell me that in four letters:
I will: T H A T.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: The sow came in with the saddle
text:
The sow came in with the saddle,
The little pig rocked the cradle,
The dish jumped up on the table
To see the pot swallow the ladle.
The spit that stood behind the door
Threw the pudding-stick on the floor.
"Odsplut!" said the gridiron,
"Can't you agree?
I'm the head constable,
Bring them to me!"
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: Little Robin Redbreast sat upon a tree
text:
Little Robin Redbreast sat upon a tree,
Up went the Pussy-Cat, and down went he,
Down came Pussy-Cat, away Robin ran;
Says little Robin Redbreast: "Catch me if you can!"

Little Robin Redbreast jumped upon a spade,
Pussy-Cat jumped after him, and then he was afraid.
Little Robin chirped and sang, and what did Pussy say?
Pussy-Cat said: "Mew, mew, mew," and Robin flew away.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: There was an old woman
text:
There was an old woman
Sold puddings and pies;
She went to the mill,
And dust flew in her eyes.
While through the streets,
To all she meets
She ever cries:
"Hot Pies--Hot Pies."
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: There was a crooked man
text:
There was a crooked man,
And he went a crooked mile,
He found a crooked sixpence
Against a crooked stile;
He bought a crooked cat
Which caught a crooked mouse,
And they all lived together
In a little crooked house.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: Hark! Hark
text:
Hark! Hark!
The dogs do bark,
The beggars are coming to town;
Some in rags,
Some in tags,
And some in velvet gown.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: As I was going to St. Ives
text:
As I was going to St. Ives
I met seven wives.
Every wife had seven sacks,
Every sack had seven cats,
Every cat had seven kits.
Kits, cats, sacks and wives,
How many were going to St. Ives?
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: When good King Arthur ruled his land
text:
When good King Arthur ruled his land
He was a goodly king;
He stole three pecks of barley meal
To make a bag-pudding.
A bag-pudding the king did make,
And stuffed it well with plums,
And in it put great lumps of fat
As big as my two thumbs.
The king and queen did eat thereof,
And noblemen beside,
And what they could not eat that night
The queen next morning fried.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: "Jacky, come give me your fiddle
text:
"Jacky, come give me your fiddle,
If ever you mean to thrive."
"Nay, I'll not give my fiddle
To any man alive.

"If I should give my fiddle
They'll think that I'm gone mad,
For many a joyful day
My fiddle and I have had."
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)
also_in: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston) (1833)

title: One, two, three, four, five
text:
One, two, three, four, five,
I caught a hare alive;
Six, seven, eight, nine, ten,
I let him go again.
source: Mother Goose, ill. Frederick Richardson (Volland)

title: No, no my Melodies will never die
text:
No, no my Melodies will never die,
While nurses sing, or babies cry.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: There was a mad man
text:
There was a mad man,
And he had a mad wife,
And they lived all in a mad lane!
They had three children all at a birth,
And they too were mad every one.
The father was mad,
The mother was mad,
The children all mad beside;
And upon a mad horse they all of them got,
And madly away did ride.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool
text:
Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?
Yes, marry have I, three bags full,
One for my master, and one for my dame,
And one for the little boy that lives in the lane.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: To market, to market, to buy a penny bun
text:
To market, to market, to buy a penny bun,
Home again, home again, market is done.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The man in the wilderness
text:
The man in the wilderness,
Asked me,
How many strawberries
Grew in the sea?
I answered him as I thought good,
As many red herrings
As grew in the wood.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Little Robin Redbreast
text:
Little Robin Redbreast
Sat upon a tree,
Up went the Pussy-Cat,
And down went he;
Down came Pussy-Cat,
Away Robin ran,
Says little Robin Redbreast--
Catch me if you can.
Little Robin Redbreast jumped upon a spade,
Pussy-Cat jumped after him, and then he was afraid.
Little Robin chirped and sung, and what did pussy say?
Pussy-Cat said Mew, mew mew,--and Robin flew away.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Snail, Snail
text:
Snail, Snail,
Come out of your hole,
Or else I'll beat you black as a coal.
Snail, Snail,
Put out your head,
Or else I'll beat you till you're dead.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Charley Wag
text:
Charley Wag,
Ate the pudding and left the bag.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Sing, Sing!--What shall I sing
text:
Sing, Sing!--What shall I sing?
The Cat's run away with the Pudding-Bag String.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Cushy Cow bonny, let down your milk
text:
Cushy Cow bonny, let down your milk,
And I will give you a gown of silk,
A gown of silk and a silver tee,
If you'll let down your milk to me.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Fa, Fe, Fi, Fo, Fum
text:
Fa, Fe, Fi, Fo, Fum!
I smell the blood of an Englishman.
Be he live or be he dead,
I'll grind his bones to make me bread.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Richard and Robin were two pretty men
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Round about, round about
text:
Round about, round about,
Gooseberry Pie,
My father loves good ale,
And so do I.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Sweep, sweep
text:
Sweep, sweep,
Chimney sweep,
From the bottom to the top,
Sweep all up,
Chimney sweep,
From the bottom to the top.

Climb by rope,
Or climb by ladder,
Without either,
I'll climb farther.

One misty, moisty morning,
When cloudy was the weather,
I chanced to meet an old man clothed all in leather.
He began to compliment, and I began to grin,
How do you do, and how do you do?
And how do you do again?
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: In April's sweet month
text:
In April's sweet month,
When the leaves 'gin to spring,
Little lambs skip like fairies
And birds build and sing.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: There was an old woman tost up in a blanket
text:
There was an old woman tost up in a blanket,
Seventy times as high as the moon,
What she did there, I cannot tell you,
but in her hand she carried a broom.
Old woman, old woman, old woman, said I,
O whither, O whither, O whither so high?
To sweep the cobwebs from the sky,
And I shall be back again by and by.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Shoe the horse, and shoe the mare
text:
Shoe the horse, and shoe the mare,
But let the little colt go bare.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: As I was going to Derby upon a market day
text:
As I was going to Derby upon a market day,
I met the finest ram, sir, that ever fed on hay,
On hay, on hay, on hay,
I met the finest ram, sir, that ever fed on hay.

This ram was fat behind, sir; this ram was fat before;
This ram was ten yards round, sir; indeed he was not more.
No more, no more, no more;
This ram was ten yards round, sir; indeed he was no more.

The horns grew on his head, sir, they were so wondrous high,
As I've been plainly told, sir, they reached up to the sky.
The sky, the sky, the sky,
As I've been plainly told, sir, they reached up to the sky.

The tail grew on his back, sir, was six yards and an ell,
And it was sent to Derby to toll the market bell,
The bell, the bell, the bell,
And it was sent to Derby to toll the market bell.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The Cuckoo is a bonny bird
text:
The Cuckoo is a bonny bird,
She sings as she flies,
She brings us good tidings,
And tells us no lies.

She sucks little bird's eggs
To make her voice clear,
And never cries Cuckoo!
Till Spring of the year.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Lavender blue, and Rosemary green
text:
Lavender blue, and Rosemary green,
When I am king, you shall be queen,
Call up my maids at four of the clock,
Some to the wheel, and some to the rock,
Some to make hay, and some to shell corn,
And you and I shall keep the bed warm.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The lion and the Unicorn
text:
The lion and the Unicorn
Were fighting for the crown--
The lion beat the unicorn
All about the town.
Some gave them white bread,
And some gave them brown,
Some gave them plum-cake,
And sent them out of town.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Little Johnny Pringle had a little Pig
text:
Little Johnny Pringle had a little Pig.
It was very little, so was not very big.
As it was playing beneath the shed,
In half a minute poor Piggy was dead.
So Johnny Pringle he sat down and cried,
And Betty Pringle she laid down and died.
There is the history of one, two and three,
Johnny Pringle, Betty Pringle, and Piggy Wiggie.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Smiling girls, rosy boys
text:
Smiling girls, rosy boys,
Come and buy my little toys,
Monkeys made of gingerbread
And sugar horses tinted red.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Hey rub-a-dub, ho rub-a-dub, three maids in a tub
text:
Hey rub-a-dub, ho rub-a-dub, three maids in a tub,
And who do you think was there?
The butcher, the baker, the candlestick-maker,
And all of them gone to the fair.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: To Be Sung In A High Wind.
text:
Arthur O'Bower has broken his band,
And he comes roaring up the land,
King of Scots with all his power
Never can turn Sir Arthur O'Bower.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Daffy-down-dilly is new come to town
text:
Daffy-down-dilly is new come to town,
With a petticoat green, and a bright yellow gown,
And her white blossoms are peeping around.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: There was an old woman, and what do you think
text:
There was an old woman, and what do you think?
She liv'd upon nothing--but victuals and drink:
Victuals and drink were the chief of her diet,
And yet this old lady scarce ever was quiet.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The rose is red, the violet is blue
text:
The rose is red, the violet is blue,
The gillyflower sweet--and so are you.
These are the words you have me say
For a pair of new gloves on Easter-day.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Great A, little a, bouncing B
text:
Great A, little a, bouncing B,
The Cat's in the cupboard, and she can't see.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The little black dog ran round the house
text:
The little black dog ran round the house,
And set the bull a roaring,
And drove the monkey in the boat,
Who set the oar a rowing,
And scared the cock upon the rock,
Who cracked his throat with crowing.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Oh, what a sweet little white Mouse
text:
Oh, what a sweet little white Mouse!
Oh, what a dear little bright Mouse!
With his eyes of pink,
Going winky-wink,
Oh, what a sweet little white Mouse.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: My little Pink
text:
My little Pink,
I suppose you think,
I cannot do without you,
I'll let you know
Before I go,
How little I care about you.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Tell tale tit, your tongue shall be slit
text:
Tell tale tit, your tongue shall be slit,
And all the dogs in our town shall have a bit.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Dear Sensibility, O la
text:
Dear Sensibility, O la!
I heard a little lamb cry, baa!
Says I, "So you have lost mamma?"
"Ah!"

The little lamb, as I said so,
Frisking about the fields did go,
And, frisking, trod upon my toe.
"Oh!"
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Pease porridge hot, pease porridge cold
text:
Pease porridge hot, pease porridge cold,
Pease porridge in the pot nine days old.
Can you spell that with four letters?
Yes, I can--T H A T.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: As I was going to sell my eggs
text:
As I was going to sell my eggs,
I met a thief with bandy legs,
Bandy legs and crooked toes,
I tript up his heels, and he fell on his nose.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Old mistress McShuttle
text:
Old mistress McShuttle
Lived in a coal-scuttle,
Along with her dog and her cat;
What they ate I can't tell,
But 'tis known very well,
That none of the party were fat.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Pussy sits behind the log
text:
Pussy sits behind the log,
How can she be fair?
Then comes in the little dog,
Pussy, are you there?
So, so, dear mistress Pussy,
Pray tell me how you do?
I thank you, little dog,
I'm very well just now.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Pat a cake, pat a cake
text:
Pat a cake, pat a cake,
Baker's man!
So I do, master, as fast as I can.
Pat it, and prick it,
And mark it with T,
And then it will serve
For Tommy and me.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Ding--dong--bell, the cat's in the well
text:
Ding--dong--bell, the cat's in the well,
Who put her in? little Johnny Green.
Who pulled her out? great Johnny Stout.
What a naughty boy was that,
To drown poor pussy cat;
Who never did him any harm,
And killed the mice in his father's barn.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Lazy Tom with jacket blue
text:
Lazy Tom with jacket blue,
Stole his father's gouty shoe.
The worst of harm that dad can wish him,
Is his gouty shoe may fit him.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Bonny lass! bonny lass
text:
Bonny lass! bonny lass!
Will you be mine?
You shall neither wash dishes
Nor serve the wine,
But sit on a cushion and sew up a seam,
And you shall have strawberries, sugar, and cream.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Dingty diddledy, my mammy's maid
text:
Dingty diddledy, my mammy's maid,
She stole oranges, I am afraid:
Some in her pocket, some in her sleeve,
She stole oranges, I do believe.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Hush-a-bye, baby, lie still with thy daddy
text:
Hush-a-bye, baby, lie still with thy daddy,
Thy mammy is gone to the mill,
To get some meal to bake a cake;
So pray, my dear baby, lie still.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Little lad, little lad
text:
Little lad, little lad,
Where were you born?
Far off in Lancashire, under a thorn,
Where they sup butter-milk
With a ram's horn;
And a pumpkin scoop'd,
With a yellow rim,
Is the bonny bowl they breakfast in.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Shake a leg, wag a leg, when will you gang
text:
Shake a leg, wag a leg, when will you gang?
At midsummer, mother, when the days are lang.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: See saw, sacradown, sacradown
text:
See saw, sacradown, sacradown,
Which is the way to Boston town?
One foot up, the other foot down,
That is the way to Boston town.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Tom Brown's two little Indian boys
text:
Tom Brown's two little Indian boys,
One ran away,
The other would n't stay,
Tom Brown's two little Indian boys.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Hop away, skip away, my baby wants to play
text:
Hop away, skip away, my baby wants to play.
My baby wants to play every day.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Bow, wow, wow, whose dog art thou
text:
Bow, wow, wow, whose dog art thou?
Little Tom Tinker's dog, bow, wow, wow.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Bobby Shaftoe's gone to sea
text:
Bobby Shaftoe's gone to sea,
Silver buckles on his knee;
He'll come back and marry me,
Pretty Bobby Shaftoe.

Bobby Shaftoe's fat and fair,
Combing down his yellow hair,
He's my love forevermore,
Pretty Bobby Shaftoe.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Boys and girls, come out to play
text:
Boys and girls, come out to play,
The moon does shine as bright as day,
Leave your supper, and leave your sleep,
And meet your playfellows in the street;
Come with a whoop, and come with a call,
And come with a good will, or not at all.
Up the ladder and down the wall,
A halfpenny roll will serve us all.
You find milk and I'll find flour,
And we'll have pudding in half an hour.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Ride a cock horse to Banbury-cross
text:
Ride a cock horse to Banbury-cross
To see what Tommy can buy;
A penny white loaf, a penny white cake,
And a two penny apple pie.

Ride a cock hose to Shrewsbury-cross,
To buy little Johnny a galloping horse
It trots behind and it ambles before,
And Johnny shall ride till he can ride no more.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Jemmy Jed went into a shed
text:
Jemmy Jed went into a shed,
And made a ted of straw his bed;
An owl came out and flew about,
And Jimmy Jed up stakes and fled.
Wasn't Jimmy Jed a staring fool,
Born in the woods to be scar'd by an owl?
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Oh I am so happy
text:
Oh I am so happy,
A little girl said,
As she sprang like a lark
From her low trundle bed.
It is morning, bright morning,
Good morning, Papa!
Oh give me one kiss,
For good morning, Mamma!
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: There was an old man in a velvet coat
text:
There was an old man in a velvet coat,
He kiss'd a maid and gave her groat;
The groat was crack'd and would not go.
Ah, old man, do you serve me so?
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Wash me and comb me
text:
Wash me and comb me
And lay me down softly,
And set me a bank to dry,
That I may look pretty,
When some one comes by.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Up in the green orchard there is a green tree
text:
Up in the green orchard there is a green tree,
The finest of pippins that ever you see;
The apples are ripe, and ready to fall,
And Reuben and Robin shall gather them all.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Jog on, jog on, the footpath way
text:
Jog on, jog on, the footpath way,
And merrily jump the style, boys,
A merry heart goes all the day,
Your sad one tires in a mile, boys.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: I will sing you a song
text:
I will sing you a song
Of the days that are long,
Of the woodcock and the sparrow,
Of the little dog that burnt his tail,
And he shall be whipt to-morrow.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: I had a little Doll
text:
I had a little Doll,
The prettiest ever seen,
She washed me the dishes,
And kept the house clean.
She went to the mill
To fetch me some flour,
And always got it home
In less than an hour;
She baked me my bread,
She brewed me my ale,
She sat by the fire
And told many a fine tale.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: When I was a little he
text:
When I was a little he,
My mother took me on her knee,
Smiles and kisses gave with joy,
And call'd me oft her darling boy.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Charley loves good cake and ale
text:
Charley loves good cake and ale,
Charley loves good candy,
Charley loves to kiss the girls,
When they are clean and handy.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: John O'Gudgeon he was a wild man
text:
John O'Gudgeon he was a wild man,
He whipt his children now and then,
When he whipt them, he made them dance,
Out of Ireland into France.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The girl in the lane
text:
The girl in the lane,
That couldn't speak plain,
Cried, Gobble, gobble, gobble;
The man on the hill,
That couldn't stand still,
Went, hobble, hobble, hobble.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Hey ding a ding, ding, I heard a bird sing
text:
Hey ding a ding, ding, I heard a bird sing,
The parliament soldiers are gone to the king.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Pibroch of Donnel Dhu
text:
Pibroch of Donnel Dhu,
Pibroch of Donnel,
Wake thy voice anew,
Summon Clan-Connel.
Come away, come away,
Hark to the summons!
Come in your war array,
Gentles and commons!

Come as the winds come,
When forests are rended,
Come as the waves come,
When navies are stranded.
Faster come, faster come, faster and faster,
Chief, vassal, page and groom,
Tenent and master.

Fast they come, fast they come,
See how they gather!
Wide waves the eagle plume blended with heather.
Cast your plaids, draw your blades,
Forward each man set!
Pibroch of Donnel Dhu, now for the onset!
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The sow came in with the saddle
text:
The sow came in with the saddle,
The little pig rock'd the cradle,
The dish jump'd up on the table
To see the pot swallow the ladle.
The spit that stood behind the door
Threw the pudding-stick on the floor.
Odsplut! said the gridiron,
Can't you agree?
I'm the head constable,
Bring them to me.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: Little Tommy Tucker
text:
Little Tommy Tucker,
Sing for your supper:
What shall I sing?
White bread and butter.
How shall I cut it
Without any knife?
How shall I marry
Without any wife?
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Hiccory, diccory, dock
text:
Hiccory, diccory, dock,
The mouse run up the clock;
The clock struck one, and down he run,
Hiccory, diccory, dock.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Away, pretty robin, fly home to your nest
text:
Away, pretty robin, fly home to your nest,
To make you my captive I still should like best,
And feed you with worms and with bread:
Your eyes are so sparkling, your feathers so soft,
Your little wings flutter so pretty aloft,
And your breast is all cover'd with red.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: See saw, Jack-a-daw
text:
See saw, Jack-a-daw,
Johnny shall have a new master;
Johnny shall have but a penny a day,
Because he can work no faster.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: We're three brethren out of Spain
text:
We're three brethren out of Spain,
Come to court your daughter Jane.

My daughter Jane she is too young,
She has no skill in a flattering tongue.

Be she young or be she old,
It's for her gold she must be sold,
So fare you well, my lady gay,
We shall return another day.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: This is the way the ladies ride
text:
This is the way the ladies ride,
Prim, prim, prim;
This is the way the gentlemen ride,
Trim, trim, trim.
Presently come the country-folks,
Hobbledy gee, hobbledy gee.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: One,                     Six
text:
One,                     Six,
Two,                     Seven,
Three,                   Eight,
Four,                    Nine,
Five,                    Ten,
I caught a hare alive.    I let it go again.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Cock a doodle doo
text:
Cock a doodle doo,
My dame has lost her shoe;
My master's lost his fiddlestick,
And knows not what to do.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: What care I how black he be
text:
What care I how black he be?
Twenty pounds will marry me
If twenty won't, forty shall,
I'm my mother's bouncing girl.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Milk-man, milk-man, where have you been
text:
Milk-man, milk-man, where have you been?
In Buttermilk channel up to my chin,
I spilt my milk, and I spoilt my clothes,
And got a long icicle hung to my nose.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: The little Robin grieves
text:
The little Robin grieves
When the snow is on the ground,
For the trees have no leaves,
And no berries can be found.

The air is cold, the worms are hid,
For Robin here what can be done?
Let's strow around some crumbs of bread,
And then he'll live till snow is gone.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: Little Jack Nory
text:
Little Jack Nory
Told me a story
How he tried
Cock-horse to ride,
Sword and scabbard by his side,
Saddle, leaden spurs and switches,
His pocket tight
With cents all bright,
Marbles, tops, puzzles, props,
Now he's put in jacket and breeches.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: There were two blackbirds sitting on a hill
text:
There were two blackbirds sitting on a hill,
One name Jack, and the other name Jill;
Fly away, Jack--fly away, Jill,
Come again, Jack--come again, Jill.
source: The Only True Mother Goose Melodies (Munroe & Francis, Boston)

title: When good king Arthur ruled this land
text:
When good king Arthur ruled this land,
He was a goodly king;
He stole three pecks of barley-meal,
To make a bag-pudding.

A bag-pudding the king did make,
And stuff'd it well with plums:
And in it put great lumps of fat,
As big as my two thumbs.

The king and queen did eat thereof,
And noblemen beside;
And what they could not eat that night,
The queen next morning fried.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [The following song relating to Robin Hood, the celebrated
text:
[The following song relating to Robin Hood, the celebrated
outlaw, is well known at Worksop, in Nottinghamshire, where it
constitutes one of the nursery series.]

Robin Hood, Robin Hood,
Is in the mickle wood!
Little John, Little John,
He to the town is gone.

Robin Hood, Robin Hood,
Is telling his beads,
All in the green wood,
Among the green weeds.

Little John, Little John,
If he comes no more,
Robin Hood, Robin Hood,
He will fret full sore!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: The king of France, with twenty thousand men
text:
The king of France, with twenty thousand men,
Went up the hill, and then came down again;
The king of Spain, with twenty thousand more,
Climb'd the same hill the French had climb'd before.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: At the siege of Belle-isle
text:
At the siege of Belle-isle
I was there all the while,
All the while, all the while,
At the siege of Belle-isle.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Good Queen Bess was a glorious dame
text:
Good Queen Bess was a glorious dame,
When bonny King Jemmy from Scotland came;
We'll pepper their bodies,
Their peaceable noddies,
And give them a crack of the crown!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Over the water, and over the lee
text:
Over the water, and over the lee,
And over the water to Charley.
Charley loves good ale and wine,
And Charley loves good brandy,
And Charley loves a pretty girl,
As sweet as sugar-candy.

Over the water, and over the sea,
And over the water to Charley,
I'll have none of your nasty beef,
Nor I'll have none of your barley;
But I'll have some of your very best flour;
To make a white cake for my Charley.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: High diddle ding
text:
High diddle ding,
Did you hear the bells ring?
The parliament soldiers are gone to the king!
Some they did laugh, some they did cry,
To see the parliament soldiers pass by.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: High ding a ding, and ho ding a ding
text:
High ding a ding, and ho ding a ding,
The parliament soldiers are gone to the king;
Some with new beavers, some with new bands,
The parliament soldiers are all to be hang'd.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [The following is a fragment of a song on the subject, which
text:
[The following is a fragment of a song on the subject, which
was introduced by Russell in the character of Jerry Sneak.]

Poor old Robinson Crusoe!
Poor old Robinson Crusoe!
They made him a coat
Of an old nanny goat,
I wonder how they could do so!
With a ring a ting tang,
And a ring a ting tang,
Poor old Robinson Crusoe!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [The following nursery song alludes to William III and George
text:
[The following nursery song alludes to William III and George
prince of Denmark.]

William and Mary, George and Anne,
Four such children had never a man:
They put their father to flight and shame,
And call'd their brother a shocking bad name.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Little General Monk
text:
Little General Monk
Sat upon a trunk,
Eating a crust of bread;
There fell a hot coal
And burnt in his clothes a hole,
Now General Monk is dead.
Keep always from the fire:
If it catch your attire,
You too, like Monk, will be dead.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: One, two, three
text:
One, two, three,
I love coffee,
And Billy loves tea.
How good you be,
One, two, three.
I love coffee,
And Billy loves tea.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: A, B, C, tumble down D
text:
A, B, C, tumble down D,
The cat's in the cupboard and can't see me.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: F for fig, J for jig
text:
F for fig, J for jig,
And N for knuckle bones,
I for John the waterman,
And S for sack of stones.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: One's none
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake, baker's man
text:
Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake, baker's man!
So I will, master, as fast as I can:
Pat it, and prick it, and mark it with T,
Put in the oven for Tommy and me.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: A was an archer, and shot at a frog
text:
A was an archer, and shot at a frog,
B was a butcher, and had a great dog.
C was a captain, all covered with lace,
D was a drunkard, and had a red face.
E was an esquire, with pride on his brow,
F was a farmer, and followed the plough.
G was a gamester, who had but ill luck,
H was a hunter and hunted a buck.
I was an innkeeper, who lov'd to bouse,
J was a joiner, and built up a house.
K was King William, once governed this land,
L was a lady, who had a white hand.
M was a miser, and hoarded up gold,
N was a nobleman, gallant and bold.
O was an oyster wench, and went about town,
P was a parson, and wore a black gown.
Q was a queen, who was fond of good flip,
R was a robber, and wanted a whip.
S was a sailor, and spent all he got,
T was a tinker, and mended a pot.
U was an usurer, a miserable elf,
V was a vintner, who drank all himself.
W was a watchman, and guarded the door.
X was expensive, and so became poor.
Y was a youth, that did not love school,
Z was a zany, a poor harmless fool.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: A for the ape, that we saw at the fair
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [The tale of Simple Simon forms one of the chap-books, but the
text:
[The tale of Simple Simon forms one of the chap-books, but the
following verses are those generally sung in the nursery.]

Simple Simon met a pieman
Going to the fair;
Says Simple Simon to the pieman,
"Let me taste your ware."

Says the pieman to Simple Simon,
"Show me first your penny."
Says Simple Simon to the pieman,
"Indeed I have not any."

Simple Simon went a fishing
For to catch a whale:
All the water he had got
Was in his mother's pail.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Punch and Judy
text:
Punch and Judy,
Fought for a pie,
Punch gave Judy
A sad blow on the eye.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Robin the Bobbin, the big-bellied Ben
text:
Robin the Bobbin, the big-bellied Ben,
He eat more meat than fourscore men;
He eat a cow, he eat a calf,
He eat a butcher and a half;
He eat a church, he eat a steeple,
He eat the priest and all the people!

A cow and a calf,
An ox and a half,
A church and a steeple,
And all the good people,
And yet he complain'd that his stomach wasn't full.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: My dear, do you know
text:
My dear, do you know,
How a long time ago,
Two poor little children,
Whose names I don't know,
Were stolen away on a fine summer's day,
And left in a wood, as I've heard people say.

And when it was night,
So sad was their plight,
The sun it went down,
And the moon gave no light!
They sobb'd and they sigh'd, and they bitterly cried,
And the poor little things, they lay down and died.

And when they were dead,
The Robins so red
Brought strawberry leaves,
And over them spread;
And all the day long,
They sung them this song,
"Poor babes in the wood! poor babes in the wood!
And don't you remember the babes in the wood?"
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: There was a little man
text:
There was a little man,
And he had a little gun,
And he went to the brook,
And he shot a little rook;
And he took it home
To his old wife Joan,
And told her to make up a fire,
While he went back,
To fetch the little drake;
But when he got there,
The drake was fled for fear,
And like an old novice,
He turn'd back again.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Little King Boggen he built a fine hall
text:
Little King Boggen he built a fine hall.
Pye-crust, and pastry-crust, that was the wall;
The windows were made of black-puddings and white,
And slated with pancakes--you ne'er saw the like.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: There was a jolly miller
text:
There was a jolly miller
Lived on the river Dee,
He look'd upon his pillow,
And there he saw a flee.
Oh! Mr. Flea,
You have been biting me,
And you must die:
So he crack'd his bones
Upon the stones,
And there he let him lie.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)
also_in: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition) (1886)

title: [The following two stanzas, although they belong to the same
text:
[The following two stanzas, although they belong to the same
piece, are often found separated from each other.]

Robin and Richard were two pretty men;
They laid in bed till the clock struck ten;
Then up starts Robin, and looks at the sky,
Oh! brother Richard, the sun's very high:

The bull's in the barn threshing the corn,
The cock's on the dunghill blowing his horn,
The cat's at the fire frying of fish,
The dog's in the pantry breading his dish.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: My lady Wind, my lady Wind
text:
My lady Wind, my lady Wind,
Went round about the house to find
A chink to get her foot in:
She tried the key-hole in the door,
She tried the crevice in the floor,
And drove the chimney soot in.

And then one night when it was dark,
She blew up such a tiny spark,
That all the house was pothered:
From it she raised up such a flame,
As flamed away to Belting Lane,
And White Cross folks were smothered.

And thus when once, my little dears,
A whisper reaches itching ears,
The same will come, you'll find:
Take my advice, restrain the tongue,
Remember what old nurse has sung
Of busy lady Wind!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Old Abram Brown is dead and gone
text:
Old Abram Brown is dead and gone,
You'll never see him more;
He used to wear a long brown coat,
That button'd down before.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: A dog and a cock
text:
A dog and a cock,
A journey once took,
They travell'd along till 'twas late;
The dog he made free
In the hollow of a tree,
And the cock on the boughs of it sate.

The cock nothing knowing,
In the morn fell a crowing,
Upon which comes a fox to the tree;
Says he, I declare,
Your voice is above,
All the creatures I ever did see.

Oh! would you come down
I the fav'rite might own,
Said the cock, there's a porter below;
If you will go in,
I promise I'll come down.
So he went--and was worried for it too.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Little Tom Tittlemouse
text:
Little Tom Tittlemouse,
Lived in a bell-house;
The bell-house broke,
And Tom Tittlemouse woke.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Tommy kept a chandler's shop
text:
Tommy kept a chandler's shop,
Richard went to buy a mop,
Tommy gave him such a knock,
That sent him out of his chandler's shop,
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Pemmy was a pretty girl
text:
Pemmy was a pretty girl,
But Fanny was a better;
Pemmy looked like any churl,
When little Fanny let her.

Pemmy had a pretty nose,
But Fanny had a better;
Pemmy oft would come to blows,
But Fanny would not let her.

Pemmy had a pretty doll,
But Fanny had a better;
Pemmy chatter'd like a poll,
When little Fanny let her.

Pemmy had a pretty song,
But Fanny had a better;
Pemmy would sing all day long,
But Fanny would not let her.

Pemmy lov'd a pretty lad,
And Fanny lov'd a better;
And Pemmy wanted for to wed,
But Fanny would not let her.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: There was a king and he had three daughter
text:
There was a king and he had three daughter,
And they all lived in a basin of water;
The basin bended,
My story's ended.
If the basin had been stronger,
My story would have been longer.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: The man in the moon
text:
The man in the moon,
Came tumbling down,
And ask'd his way to Norwich,
He went by the south,
And burnt his mouth
With supping cold pease-porridge.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Our saucy boy Dick
text:
Our saucy boy Dick,
Had a nice little stick
Cut from a hawthorn tree;
And with this pretty stick,
He thought he could beat
A boy much bigger than he.

But the boy turned round,
And hit him a rebound,
Which did so frighten poor Dick,
That, without more delay,
He ran quite away,
And over a hedge he jumped quick.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Moss was a little man, and a little mare did buy
text:
Moss was a little man, and a little mare did buy,
For kicking and for sprawling none her could come nigh;
She could trot, she could amble, and could canter here and there,
But one night she strayed away--so Moss lost his mare.

Moss got up next morning to catch her fast asleep,
And round about the frosty fields so nimbly he did creep.
Dead in a ditch he found her, and glad to find her there,
So I'll tell you by and bye, how Moss caught his mare.

Rise! stupid, rise! he thus to her did say;
Arise, you beast, you drowsy beast, get up without delay,
For I must ride you to the town, so don't lie sleeping there;
He put the halter round her neck--so Moss caught his mare.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: St. Swithin's day, if thou dost rain
text:
St. Swithin's day, if thou dost rain,
For forty days it will remain:
St. Swithin's day, if thou be fair,
For forty days 'twill rain na mair.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: If wishes were horses
text:
If wishes were horses,
Beggars would ride;
If turnips were watches,
I would wear one by my side.

LXXXIII.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Nature requires five
text:
Nature requires five,
Custom gives seven!
Laziness takes nine,
And Wickedness eleven.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Three straws on a staff
text:
Three straws on a staff,
Would make a baby cry and laugh.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: When the wind is in the east
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Bounce Buckram, velvet's dear
text:
Bounce Buckram, velvet's dear;
Christmas comes but once a year.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: A man of words and not of deeds
text:
A man of words and not of deeds,
Is like a garden full of weeds;
For when the weeds begin to grow,
Then doth the garden overflow.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: He that would thrive
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: They that wash on Monday
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: A sunshiny shower
text:
A sunshiny shower,
Won't last half an hour.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As the days lengthen
text:
As the days lengthen,
So the storms strengthen.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: He that goes to see his wheat in May
text:
He that goes to see his wheat in May,
Comes weeping away.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: The mackerel's cry
text:
The mackerel's cry,
Is never long dry.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: In July
text:
In July,
Some reap rye;
In August,
If one will not the other must.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [Proverbial many years ago, when the guinea in gold was of a
text:
[Proverbial many years ago, when the guinea in gold was of a
higher value than its nominal representative in silver,]

A guinea it would sink,
And a pound it would float;
Yet I'd rather have a guinea,
Than your one pound note.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: The art of good driving 's a paradox quite
text:
The art of good driving 's a paradox quite,
Though custom has prov'd it so long;
If you go to the left, you're sure to go right,
If you go to the right, you go wrong.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Friday night's dream
text:
Friday night's dream
On the Saturday told,
Is sure to come true,
Be it never so old.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: When the sand doth feed the clay
text:
When the sand doth feed the clay,
England woe and well-a-day!
But when the clay doth feed the sand,
Then it is well with Angle-land.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Tell tale, tit
text:
Tell tale, tit!
Your tongue shall be slit,
And all the dogs in the town
Shall have a little bit.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Birch and green holly, boys
text:
Birch and green holly, boys,
Birch and green holly.
If you get beaten, boys,
'Twill be your own folly.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: When V and I together meet
text:
When V and I together meet,
They make the number Six compleat.
When I with V doth meet once more,
Then 'tis they Two can make but Four
And when that V from I is gone,
Alas! poor I can make but One.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: The rose is red, the grass is green
text:
The rose is red, the grass is green;
And in this book my name is seen.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Cross patch
text:
Cross patch,
Draw the latch,
Sit by the fire and spin;
Take a cup,
And drink it up,
Then call your neighbours in.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Speak when you're spoken to
text:
Speak when you're spoken to,
Come when one call;
Shut the door after you,
And turn to the wall!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Doctor Faustus was a good man
text:
Doctor Faustus was a good man,
He whipt his scholars now and then;
When he whipp'd them he made them dance,
Out of Scotland into France,
Out of France into Spain,
And then he whipp'd them back again!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: When I was a little boy, I had but little wit
text:
When I was a little boy, I had but little wit
It is some time ago, and I've no more yet;
Nor ever ever shall, until that I die,
For the longer I live, the more fool am I.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Oh, where are you going
text:
Oh, where are you going,
My pretty maiden fair,
With your red rosy cheeks,
And your coal-black hair?
I'm going a-milking,
Kind sir, says she;
And it's dabbling in the dew,
Where you'll find me.

May I go with you,
My pretty maiden fair, &c.
Oh, you may go with me,
Kind sir, says she, &c.

If I should chance to kiss you,
My pretty maiden fair, &c.
The wind may take it off again,
Kind sir, says she, &c.

And what is your father,
My pretty maiden fair, &c.
My father is a farmer,
Kind sir, says she, &c.

And what is your mother,
My pretty maiden fair, &c.
My mother is a dairy-maid,
Kind sir, says she, &c.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: The fox and his wife they had a great strife
text:
The fox and his wife they had a great strife,
They never eat mustard in all their whole life;
They eat their meat without fork or knife,
And loved to be picking a bone, e-ho!

The fox jumped up on a moonlight night;
The stars they were shining, and all things bright;
Oh, ho! said the fox, it's a very fine night
For me to go through the town, e-ho!

The fox when he came to yonder stile,
He lifted his lugs and he listened a while!
Oh, ho! said the fox, it's but a short mile
From this unto yonder wee town, e-ho!

The fox when he came to the farmer's gate,
Who should he see but the farmer's drake;
I love you well for your master's sake,
And long to be picking your bone, e-ho!

The gray goose she ran round the hay-stack,
Oh, ho! said the fox, you are very fat;
You'll grease my beard and ride on my back
From this into yonder wee town, e-ho!

Old Gammer Hipple-hopple hopped out of bed,
She opened the casement, and popped out her head;
Oh! husband, oh! husband, the gray goose is dead,
And the fox is gone through the town, oh!

Then the old man got up in his red cap,
And swore he would catch the fox in a trap;
But the fox was too cunning, and gave him the slip,
And ran thro' the town, the town, oh!

When he got to the top of the hill,
He blew his trumpet both loud and shrill,
For joy that he was safe
Thro' the town, oh!

When the fox came back to his den,
He had young ones both nine and ten,
"You're welcome home, daddy, you may go again,
If you bring us such nice meat
From the town, oh!"
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Says t'auld man tit oak tree
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: About the bush, Willy
text:
About the bush, Willy,
About the bee-hive,
About the bush, Willy,
I'll meet thee alive.

Then to my ten shillings,
Add you but a groat,
I'll go to Newcastle,
And buy a new coat.

Five and five shillings,
Five and a crown;
Five and five shillings,
Will buy a new gown.

Five and five shillings,
Five and a groat;
Five and five shillings,
Will buy a new coat.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: A pretty little girl in a round-eared cap
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: My father he died, but I can't tell you how
text:
My father he died, but I can't tell you how,
He left me six horses to drive in my plough:
With my wing wang waddle oh,
Jack sing saddle oh,
Blowsey boys bubble oh,
Under the broom.

I sold my six horses and I bought me a cow;
I'd fain have made a fortune but did not know how:
With my, &c.

I sold my cow, and I bought me a calf;
I'd fain have made a fortune, but lost the best half:
With my, &c.

I sold my calf, and I bought me a cat;
A pretty thing she was, in my chimney corner sat:
With my, &c.

I sold my cat, and bought me a mouse;
He carried fire in his tail, and burnt down my house:
With my, &c.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Jeanie come tie my
text:
Jeanie come tie my,
Jeanie come tie my,
Jeanie come tie my bonnie cravat;
I've tied it behind,
I've tied it before,
And I've tied it so often, I'll tie it no more.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Trip upon trenchers, and dance upon dishes
text:
Trip upon trenchers, and dance upon dishes,
My mother sent me for some barm, some barm;
She bid me tread lightly, and come again quickly,
For fear the young men should do me some harm.
Yet didn't you see, yet didn't you see,
What naughty tricks they put upon me:

They broke my pitcher,
And spilt the water,
And huff'd my mother,
And chid her daughter,
And kiss'd my sister instead of me.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As I was walking o'er little Moorfields
text:
As I was walking o'er little Moorfields,
I saw St. Paul's a running on wheels,
With a fee, fo, fum.
Then for further frolics I'll go to France.
While Jack shall sing and his wife shall dance,
With a fee, fo fum.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [From W. Wager's play, called 'The longer thou livest, the
text:
[From W. Wager's play, called 'The longer thou livest, the
more foole thou art,' 4to, Lond.]

The white dove sat on the castle wall,
I bend my bow and shoot her I shall;
I put her in my glove both feathers and all;
I laid my bridle upon the shelf,
If you will any more, sing it yourself.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: London bridge is broken down
text:
London bridge is broken down,
Dance o'er my lady lee;
London bridge is broken down,
With a gay lady.

How shall we build it up again?
Dance o'er my lady lee;
How shall we build it up again?
With a gay lady.

Silver and gold will be stole away,
Dance o'er my lady lee;
Silver and gold will be stole away,
With a gay lady.

Build it up again with iron and steel,
Dance o'er my lady lee;
Build it up with iron and steel,
With a gay lady.

Iron and steel will bend and bow,
Dance o'er my lady lee;
Iron and steel will bend and bow,
With a gay lady.

Build it up with wood and clay,
Dance o'er my lady lee;
Build it up with wood and clay,
With a gay lady.

Wood and clay will wash away,
Dance o'er my lady lee;
Wood and clay will wash away,
With a gay lady.

Build it up with stone so strong,
Dance o'er my lady lee;
Huzza! 'twill last for ages long,
With a gay lady.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: I love sixpence, pretty little sixpence
text:
I love sixpence, pretty little sixpence,
I love sixpence better than my life;
I spent a penny of it, I spent another,
And took fourpence home to my wife.

Oh, my little fourpence, pretty little fourpence,
I love fourpence better than my life;
I spent a penny of it, I spent another,
And I took twopence home to my wife.

Oh, my little twopence, my pretty little twopence,
I love twopence better than my life;
I spent a penny of it, I spent another,
And I took nothing home to my wife.

Oh, my little nothing, my pretty little nothing,
What will nothing buy for my wife?
I have nothing, I spend nothing,
I love nothing better than my wife.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Merry are the bells, and merry would they ring
text:
Merry are the bells, and merry would they ring,
Merry was myself, and merry could I sing;
With a merry ding-dong, happy, gay, and free,
And a merry sing-song, happy let us be!

Waddle goes your gait, and hollow are your hose,
Noddle goes your pate, and purple is your nose;
Merry is your sing-song, happy, gay, and free,
With a merry ding-dong, happy let us be!

Merry have we met, and merry have we been,
Merry let us part, and merry meet again;
With our merry sing-song, happy, gay, and free,
And a merry ding-dong, happy let us be!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Wooley Foster has gone to sea
text:
Wooley Foster has gone to sea,
With silver buckles at his knee,
When he comes back he'll marry me,--
Bonny Wooley Foster!

Wooley Foster has a cow,
Black and white about the mow,
Open the gates and let her through,
Wooley Foster's ain cow!

Wooley Foster has a hen,
Cockle button, cockle ben,
She lay eggs for gentlemen,
But none for Wooley Foster!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [The following catch is found in Ben Jonson's 'Masque of
text:
[The following catch is found in Ben Jonson's 'Masque of
Oberon,' and is a most common nursery song at the present
day.]

Buz, quoth the blue fly,
Hum, quoth the bee,
Buz and hum they cry,
And so do we:
In his ear, in his nose,
Thus, do you see?
He ate the dormouse,
Else it was he.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As I was going up the hill
text:
As I was going up the hill,
I met with Jack the piper,
And all the tunes that he could play
Was "Tie up your petticoats tighter."

I tied them once, I tied them twice,
I tied them three times over;
And all the songs that he could sing
Was "Carry me safe to Dover."
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: How does my lady's garden grow
text:
How does my lady's garden grow?
How does my lady's garden grow?
With cockle shells, and silver bells,
And pretty maids all of a row.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As I was going along, long, long
text:
As I was going along, long, long,
A singing a comical song, song, song,
The lane that I went was so long, long, long,
And the song that I sung was as long, long, long,
And so I went singing along.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: My father left me three acres of land
text:
My father left me three acres of land,
Sing ivy, sing ivy;
My father left me three acres of land,
Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!

I ploughed it with a ram's horn,
Sing ivy, sing ivy;
And sowed it all over with one pepper corn,
Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!

I harrowed it with a bramble bush,
Sing ivy, sing ivy;
And reaped it with my little penknife,
Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!

I got the mice to carry it to the barn,
Sing ivy, &c.
And thrashed it with a goose's quill,
Sing holly, &c.

I got the cat to carry it to the mill,
Sing ivy, &c.
The miller he swore he would have her paw,
And the cat she swore she would scratch his face,
Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: [Song of a little boy while passing his hour of solitude in a
text:
[Song of a little boy while passing his hour of solitude in a
corn-field.]

Awa' birds, away!
Take a little, and leave a little,
And do not come again;
For if you do,
I will shoot you through,
And there is an end of you.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Whistle, daughter, whistle, whistle daughter dear
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: I'll sing you a song
text:
I'll sing you a song,
Though not very long,
Yet I think it as pretty as any,
Put your hand in your purse,
You'll never be worse,
And give the poor singer a penny.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Dame, get up and bake your pies
text:
Dame, get up and bake your pies,
Bake your pies, bake your pies;
Dame, get up and bake your pies,
On Christmas-day in the morning.

Dame, what makes your maidens lie,
Maidens lie, maidens lie;
Dame, what makes your maidens lie,
On Christmas-day in the morning?

Dame, what makes your ducks to die,
Ducks to die, ducks to die;
Dame, what makes your ducks to die,
On Christmas-day in the morning?

Their wings are cut and they cannot fly,
Cannot fly, cannot fly;
Their wings are cut and they cannot fly,
On Christmas-day in the morning.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Hick-a-more, Hack-a-more
text:
Hick-a-more, Hack-a-more,
On the king's kitchen-door;
All the king's horses,
And all the king's men,
Couldn't drive Hick-a-more, Hack-a-more,
Off the king's kitchen-door!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: When I was taken from the fair body
text:
When I was taken from the fair body,
They then cut off my head,
And thus my shape was altered;
It's I that make peace between king and king,
And many a true lover glad:
All this I do and ten times more,
And more I could do still,
But nothing can I do,
Without my guider's will.

CLXXXVII.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As I look'd out o' my chamber window
text:
As I look'd out o' my chamber window
I heard something fall;
I sent my maid to pick it up,
But she couldn't pick it all.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Ten and ten and twice eleven
text:
Ten and ten and twice eleven,
Take out six and put in seven;
Go to the green and fetch eighteen,
And drop one a coming.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As soft as silk, as white as milk
text:
As soft as silk, as white as milk,
As bitter as gall, a thick wall,
And a green coat covers me all.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As I was going o'er Tipple Tine
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Arthur O'Bower has broken his band
text:
Arthur O'Bower has broken his band,
He comes roaring up the land;--
The King of Scots, with all his power,
Cannot turn Arthur of the Bower!
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Make three-fourths of a cross
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Every lady in this land
text:
Every lady in this land
Has twenty nails upon each hand,
Five and twenty hands and feet,
All this is true without deceit.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: I have a little sister, they call her peep, peep
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: In marble walls as white as milk
text:
In marble walls as white as milk,
Lined with a skin as soft as silk;
Within a fountain crystal clear,
A golden apple doth appear.
No doors there are to this strong-hold.
Yet things break in and steal the gold.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: What shoe-maker makes shoes without leather
text:
What shoe-maker makes shoes without leather,
With all the four elements put together?
Fire and water, earth and air;
Ev'ry customer has two pair.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Higgledy piggledy
text:
Higgledy piggledy
Here we lie,
Pick'd and pluck'd,
And put in a pie.
My first is snapping, snarling, growling,
My second's industrious, romping, and prowling.
Higgledy piggledy
Here we lie,
Pick'd and pluck'd,
And put in a pie.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: There was a man who had no eyes
text:
There was a man who had no eyes,
He went abroad to view the skies;
He saw a tree with apples on it,
He took no apples off, yet left no apples on it.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: The moon nine days old
text:
The moon nine days old,
The next sign to cancer;
Pat rat without a tail;--
And now, sir, for your answer,
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Little Nancy Etticoat
text:
Little Nancy Etticoat,
In a white petticoat,
And a red nose;
The longer she stands,
The shorter she grows.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Congeal'd water and Cain's brother
text:
Congeal'd water and Cain's brother,
That was my lover's name, and no other.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Black we are, but much admired
text:
Black we are, but much admired;
Men seek for us till they are tired.
We tire the horse, but comfort man
Tell me this riddle if you can.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Humpty dumpty sate on a wall
text:
Humpty dumpty sate on a wall,
Humpty dumpty had a great fall;
Three score men and three score more
Cannot place Humpty Dumpty as he was before.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Formed long ago, yet made to-day
text:
Formed long ago, yet made to-day,
Employed while others sleep;
What few would like to give away,
Nor any wish to keep.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: As round as an apple, as deep as a cup
text:
As round as an apple, as deep as a cup,
And all the king's horses can't pull it up.
source: The Nursery Rhymes of England, J. O. Halliwell (1842; Warne edition)

title: Highty, tighty, paradighty clothed in green
text:
Highty, tighty, paradighty clothed in green,
The king could not read it, no more could the queen;
They sent for a wise man out of the East,
